n: At last the Lord answers Job — not with an explanation of his suffering, but with his presence. That God speaks at all is itself an answer to Job’s plea. Latter-day Saints understand the LORD (Jehovah) as the premortal Jesus Christ.

f.g: Small capitals render God’s covenant name YHWH (Jehovah), used here for the first time since chapters 1–2.
A storm or tempest — a common setting for God’s appearances.

n: God asks who is clouding his plan with words that lack understanding. Job has spoken honestly, but without the full picture.

f.g: Obscures God’s purpose or design.

n: God tells Job to brace himself like a man, for now God will ask the questions. Job wanted a hearing — now he has one, but on God’s terms.

f.g: Tuck up your robe into your belt — get ready for action or contest.

n: The first question: where was Job when God laid the earth’s foundations? Latter-day Saints recall that we did exist then, as spirits, though we do not remember it.

f.w: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?

n: Who determined its measurements and stretched a measuring line across it? God is pictured as a master builder.

f.g: A builder’s measuring cord.

n: What are its foundations set on, and who laid its cornerstone? The cornerstone is a familiar symbol of Christ.

When the earth was founded, the morning stars sang and all the sons of God shouted for joy. Latter-day Saints see here the premortal council, where God’s spirit children rejoiced at the plan of salvation.

f.w: all the sons of God shouted for joy

n: Who shut the sea behind doors when it burst out like a baby from the womb? The fearsome sea is pictured as God’s infant.

f.w: shut up the sea with doors

n: God wrapped the newborn sea in clouds as clothing and in darkness as a baby’s swaddling cloth.

f.g: A strip of cloth wrapped around a newborn.

n: He fixed its limits with bars and doors.

f.g: The boundary God decreed for the sea.

n: He told the sea, “This far and no farther; here your proud waves must stop.” God sets limits even on chaos.

f.w: Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further

n: Has Job ever commanded the morning to come or shown the dawn its place?

f.g: Dawn, daybreak.

n: Dawn grabs the edges of the earth like a blanket and shakes the wicked out of it — for evildoers love darkness.

f.w: that the wicked might be shaken out of it

n: In morning light the earth takes shape like clay under a seal, and its features stand out like folds in a garment.

f.g: A signet ring pressed into soft clay leaves a clear image — so dawn reveals the landscape.

n: The wicked lose their “light” — the darkness they work in — and their raised arm is broken.

f.g: An arm raised in violence or defiance.

n: Has Job traveled to the springs of the sea or walked on the floor of the deep?

f.g: The hidden sources of the ocean.

n: Has he seen the gates of death or the doors of deep darkness? God alone has authority over death. Christ himself would later open those gates.
Does Job understand how vast the earth is? Let him say so if he knows it all.
Where does light live? Where is darkness’s home?
Could Job lead them back to their homes or find the paths there?

f.g: Its territory or boundary.

n: God teases gently: surely Job knows, since he was born back then and has lived so many years! The irony humbles without crushing.
Has Job entered the storehouses where snow and hail are kept?

f.g: Storehouses — ancient poetry pictured weather kept in heavenly warehouses.

n: God holds these in reserve for times of trouble and battle.

f.w: the day of battle and war

n: What is the path to where lightning is scattered or where the east wind spreads over the earth?

f.g: Possibly lightning distributed across the sky.

n: Who carved channels for downpours and a path for the thunderstorm?

f.w: a way for the lightning of thunder

n: God sends rain even on land where no human lives. Creation isn’t only about us — God cares for places no one sees.

f.w: on the wilderness, wherein there is no man

n: He waters desolate wasteland and makes tender grass sprout.

f.w: the bud of the tender herb

n: Does the rain have a father? Who fathered the dewdrops? Only God is their source.
From whose womb did ice come, and who gave birth to the frost from the sky?

f.g: White frost.
Given birth to, produced.

n: Water hardens like stone, and the surface of the deep freezes.

f.g: Frozen hard as stone.

n: Can Job tie together the cluster of the Pleiades or loosen Orion’s belt? God moves the constellations; humans can only watch.

f.g: The “Seven Sisters,” a star cluster.
The constellation of the hunter.

n: Can he lead out the constellations in their seasons or guide the Bear with her cubs?

f.g: Probably the constellations of the zodiac or a particular star group.
Probably the Great Bear (Big Dipper) with its stars as “sons.”

n: Does Job know the laws that govern the heavens or set their rule over the earth?
Can he shout to the clouds and have them drench him with rain?

f.w: lift up thy voice to the clouds

n: Can he send lightning bolts on their way and have them report, “Here we are”?

f.g: Lightning pictured as obedient servants reporting for duty.

n: Who put wisdom in the heart or understanding in the mind? (Some translate these as birds — the ibis and rooster — said to sense weather.)

f.g: Possibly “the ibis,” a bird thought to predict the Nile’s flooding.
Possibly “the rooster,” which announces dawn.

n: Who is wise enough to count the clouds, or can tip over the water jars of heaven…

f.g: Water-skins of the sky — rain clouds.

n: …when dust becomes hard and clods of earth stick together in drought?

f.g: Dry earth clumps hard before the rain.

n: God turns to animals. Can Job hunt prey for the lioness or satisfy hungry young lions?

f.w: Wilt thou hunt the prey for the lion?

n: …when they crouch in their dens or lie in wait in the thicket?

f.g: Crouch, lie down.
Hiding place, thicket.

n: Who provides food for the raven when its chicks cry to God, wandering in hunger? God cares for even the least-regarded birds — and surely for Job.

f.w: Who provideth for the raven his food?
